doc.title: Bruce Johnstone interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2013

title: Taking over curricular jazz and the Fredonia Jazz Ensemble tension
summary: Starting at Fredonia in 2001 he met hostility from the student-run FJE, which took about four years to ease into a collegial relationship.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

Oh, no. That one’s not me.
Yeah. I’ll send you a different one.
Didn’t you send me some string stuff?

Yeah. And this is something I started at the college, ever since I came to Fredonia. Well it was strange when I came to Fredonia because FJE [Fredonia Jazz Ensemble] was still there but they had — their musicality had dropped to the point where they would sit on stage and play “Chameleon” for twenty minutes.
2001. And the rest of the people weren’t soloing. They were sitting on the stand like this or they’re bored.
Did the administration know that was happening?

I think so. And I think I was hired to bring some structure to the FJE. However, the FJE thought that I was there to destroy them, and to get out of being their exclusive club and mainstream. And I wasn’t there to do that at all. I started out with 14 kids who were brand new freshmen. We slammed a band together and played a concert three weeks after I started, in the library, which kind of shocked everybody, but it got everybody’s attention. But it took me nearly four years before the FJE stopped hating me.

You know that’s — I’d heard that through — because I graduated in ’72. FJE was a big part of our lives. And when I heard that at first I was astonished. And then I started to think about it and I said well when we were there we were all student run. They gave us a faculty advisor. And we always used to moan and bitch about —
Yeah. But I think we had a lot of pride in the fact that we were doing this. So I can see how the students might think oh, now they’re going to take it away from us.

And nobody asked me to. None of the FJE came to me and asked me. In fact they would pointedly — if I was walking down a hallway and somebody was coming the other way they would either turn or they would get as far away from me as possible. It was just rude. And so I put up with that for about four years, until most of these people who were the instigators had graduated. And now part of that 98% of the FJE have had interactions © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -15-

with me in the curricular bands, with sharing repertoires, the FJE would come to me and say do you have such and such a chart, can I borrow it. And I’d say sure, here you go. And they’ll play it. And likewise, if they’ve got something great in their library that I’d like to borrow I just go ask them to borrow it, and then give it back to them. And so I think we’re becoming more of colleagues than adversaries. So I’m very happy with the way it is. And so I’m one of the faculty advisors for the FJE and for the two big bands that they have. And it’s good, because we interact. But I don’t go and actually rehearse them. Because if I did that then their status as a student-run group would have been taken away and they’d lose all their funding. So I’ve been very supportive of them whenever I do a concert with the curricular band I’ll always advertise the fact that — come and hear the FJE when they play. So I think we’ve broken down that barrier to the point where it’s all very positive now.
